subject: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot

messages.author: 9a34d88d4b388ecb
messages.subject: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
parts:
Dear list,

Apologies for the newbie question.

I am plotting 2 variables against one other as follows:

cols <- c("LWW" = "red", "EWW" = "black")
dat = melt(mydata, measure.vars=c("EWW", "LWW"))

qplot(RW, value, xlab="Ring width (mm)", ylab="Earlywood or latewood
width (mm)", data = dat, colour=variable) +
scale_colour_manual(values = cols, breaks = c("EWW", "LWW"), labels =
c("Earlywood", "Latewood"), name="Wood Type") +
opts(legend.position=c(0.2,0.89))

However, I would like to change the plot symbols but can't see a way
to do it. I have tried experimenting with scale_shape_manual with
limited success because if I manage to change the symbols then the
legend is wrong, or I can change the symbols by mapping the shape to
the variables, but then the color scheme disappears.

Can anyone help me please?

Many thanks,

Dave

messages.author: 13ff1921a4b26560
messages.subject: Re: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
parts:
Hi Dave,
without a reproducible example I don't know what was wrong about
your legend.
If it helps, the way to collapse multiple legend sections that map the
same variable to different scales is to make the name and labels match
up between scales.
I assume that you want to specify the shapes that you are using -
otherwise change to scale_shape_discrete and remove the values call:

library(ggplot2)

fakedata <- data.frame(RW = 1:5, EWW = 0:4, LWW = 4.5:0.5)
cols <- c("LWW" = "red", "EWW" = "black")

dat <- melt(fakedata, measure.vars = c("EWW", "LWW"))


qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)", ylab = "Earlywood or
latewood width (mm)", data = dat, colour = variable, shape = variable)
+
scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = cols, breaks =
c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood")) +
scale_shape_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = c(2, 5), breaks =
c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood"))


-Allan

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
parts:
Hi:

Thanks for the reproducible example. There are some ways to make the plot more efficient, though.

I find it very useful to define the legend labels as levels of a factor in the data and assign the name I want for the legend to be its variable name in the data - all I'm really doing is relabeling the factor variable and giving it an evocative name.

dat$WoodType <- factor(dat$variable, labels = c('Earlywood', 'Latewood'))

This makes the call a lot easier, removing the need for the color scale entirely and making the scale_shape_manual call straightforward:

qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)",
       ylab = "Earlywood or latewood width (mm)", data = dat,

colour = WoodType, shape = WoodType) +
   scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 18))

I wanted to make the point size bigger, so since I use ggplot() instead, it was just easier for me to write it that way:

ggplot(dat, aes(x = RW, y = value, colour = WoodType, shape = WoodType)) +
      geom_point(size = 3) + scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 18)) +
      xlab("Ring width (mm)") +
      ylab("Earlywood or latewood width (mm)")

BTW, I got an error when I tried running your code:
> qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)", ylab = "Earlywood or
+ latewood width (mm)", data = dat, colour = variable, shape = variable)

> +
+        scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = cols, breaks =
+ c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood")) +
+        scale_shape_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = c(2, 5), breaks =

+ c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood"))
Error in +scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = cols, breaks = c("EWW",  :
  invalid argument to unary operator

I think the problem is that your cols object contained both breaks and values and you used all three (including labels) in the scale_colour_manual() call. Coordinating breaks, values and labels takes some practice, which is why it's easier to simplify the plot call as much as possible by carefully arranging the data in advance.

HTH,
Dennis
